summary: This note explains impeachment as a legislative process, drawing on the U.S. Constitution's Article One and the British system it resembles. The House of Representatives holds the sole power to impeach and the Senate the sole power to try impeachments of federal officers, with similar measures in some state constitutions. Impeachment is only the first stage, a formal statement of charges akin to an indictment, and a separate vote determines conviction, which usually requires a supermajority and results in removal from office rather than a criminal trial.
one_line: Explains impeachment as a two-stage legislative process in which charges are brought against officials and a supermajority vote decides removal from office.
key_facts: Article One of the United States Constitution gives the House of Representatives the sole power of impeachment.
Article One of the United States Constitution gives the Senate the sole power to try impeachments of officers of the U.S. national government.
Various state constitutions include similar measures allowing the state legislature to impeach the governor or other state officials.
Unlike the British system, in the United States impeachment is only the first of two stages.
Conviction during the second stage of U.S. impeachment requires a two-thirds majority vote.
Impeachment does not necessarily result in removal from office; it is only a legal statement of charges.
Impeachment is parallel to an indictment in criminal law.
An impeached official faces a second legislative vote, by the same body or another, which determines conviction or failure to convict.
Most constitutions require a supermajority to convict in impeachment proceedings.
Although the subject of the charge is criminal action, impeachment does not constitute a criminal trial.
The only question in impeachment is the removal of the individual from office and the possibility of a subsequent vote barring them from future political office in that jurisdiction.
Impeachment with respect to political office should not be confused with witness impeachment.
